sights.name: Linlithgow Palace
sights.content: Ruined but imposing medieval palace. A fort stood here in the 14th century but it and much of the town burned down. King James I rebuilt it, his successors continued to embellish it, and Mary Queen of Scots was born here in 1542. But it bec

sights.name: Blackness Castle
sights.content: Blackness was the port for the Royal Burgh of Linlithgow, so the monarchs often travelled this way, and it needed to be stoutly defended. The 15th century castle looks like a stone ship about to sail out into the Firth of Forth. Good views

sights.name: House of the Binns
sights.content: is an early 17th century mansion, now run by National Trust for Scotland, It was the home of Tam Dalyell (1932-2017), who coined the "West Lothian Question" on Scotland's position within the UK parliament. The house can be visited on guided

sights.name: Falkirk Wheel
sights.content: The Forth and Clyde Canal was completed in 1790 and its eastern extension the Union Canal reached Edinburgh in 1822. The Union ascended from the Forth and Clyde by a flight of 11 locks, which took barges a whole day to traverse and drained

sights.name: Rough Castle Fort
sights.content: Earthwork remains of a Roman fort on the [[Kilsyth#Understand

sights.name: Callendar House
sights.content: This began as a turretted house in the 14th century. It was the home of the well-connected Livingston family but they backed the Jacobites in 1715 and again in 1745 and paid the price. It was bought by a businessman, William Forbes, who gre

foodDrink.name: Benny T's
foodDrink.content: Excellent fish and chips to eat in or takeaway.

foodDrink.name: Sanam Tandoori
foodDrink.content: Decent Indian fare, good value for money.

foodDrink.name: Chianti Restaurant
foodDrink.content: This Italian restaurant gets great reviews.

sights.name: Glasgow Cathedral
sights.content: This was built in 1197 but much modified in the 13th century and is a fine example of medieval Gothic. It's dedicated to St Mungo, the city's patron saint, who is buried in the crypt. The Church of Scotland doesn't have bishops so it actual

sights.name: Glasgow Necropolis
sights.content: Dominated by the statue of John Knox, it's a pharaonic “City of the Dead”, with its grand monuments to merchants and baillies who would be as prestigious in the next world as they were in this. One fellow was so renowned that there was no n

sights.name: Glasgow Vintage Vehicle Trust
sights.hours: Open to the public on event days only, usually the first Sun of the month spring to autumn, plus an Annual Open Weekend in October. Guided tours by advance booking
sights.content: A volunteer-run charity caring for a large collection of historic buses, coaches and commercial vehicles in a working bus garage. Many of the vehicles still run, and on open days visitors can board them and take short rides. Check the websi

sights.name: George Square
sights.content: It marks the centre of this sprawling city. It was laid out in 1781 and named for King George III, since he wasn't mad at the time, though he made up for that later. In that era Glasgow expanded south from its medieval East End nucleus, ban

sights.name: City Chambers
sights.content: The City Council headquarters were built in 1888 in Italian Renaissance style. Tours take in the marble staircases, lobbies, debating chamber and banqueting hall. Public tours are conducted M-F at 10:30AM and 2:30PM. Tickets for the tour ca

sights.name: Gallery of Modern Art
sights.content: It houses rotating exhibitions of contemporary work; there isn't a permanent collection, but exhibitions generally reside for several months. In the basement is one of Glasgow's many public libraries. The building was erected in 1778 as the

sights.name: Glasgow Cross
sights.content: was the centre of the early modern city, as it expanded south from its medieval core towards the Clyde. Only the clocktower survives of the former city chambers, demolished in 1921.

sights.name: Glasgow Police Museum
sights.hours: Apr-Oct: Mon-Sat 10:30AM-4:30PM, Sun noon-4:30PM; Nov-Mar: Tue Sun 10AM-4:30PM
sights.content: Early police forces had a variety of roles that were later separated as firefighting, event security, night-watch and sanitary regulation (which often meant extorting bribes from the sex trade). Glasgow had the world's first police force fr

sights.name: Sharmanka Kinetic Theatre
sights.content: "Sharmanka" is Russian for "barrel-organ" and it's a kinetic gallery. It has dingbat machines created by Eduard Bersudsky, described somewhere between Heath Robinson and Jean Tinguely.

sights.name: St Enoch Subway Station
sights.content: A Victorian Saint Pancras Station-style anomaly in an otherwise grey square. It's the nearest Subway to Central, though you'd only use it for outlying parts. The interior is modern.

sights.name: St Andrews in the Square
sights.content: Church completed in 1756 in classical style. This closed in 1993 and became a centre for traditional Scottish music, song and dance. It still promotes those but the church itself is seldom used as a venue.

sights.name: Glasgow Green
sights.content: is the extensive green space north bank of the Clyde. It was created in 1450 as separate plots of soggy grazing land, which were combined and drained. It became an area for bleaching and drying, mass protests and inflammatory speeches, and

sights.name: People's Palace
sights.content: This is a great folk museum, telling the history of Glasgow and its people from 1750 to 2000. One of Billy Connolly's banana boots is on display. The '''Winter Gardens''' are a large adjacent glasshouse. As of May 2026, the museum and glass

sights.name: Willow Tea Rooms
sights.content: The temperance activist Kate Cranston established a chain of artistic tea rooms, where citizens (especially women) could enjoy non-alcoholic refreshments in genteel surroundings. Her designer was Charles Rennie Mackintosh, and this Sauchieh

sights.name: Glasgow School of Art
sights.content: GSA is an independent art school offering university level programmes and research in architecture, fine art and design. It also has evening classes and a summer school. However the main draw for general visitors was its Mackintosh building

sights.name: Tenement House
sights.price: Adult £8.50, conc £6, child £1, NTS / NT free
sights.content: Miss Agnes Toward was a shorthand typist who lived here 1911-1965 and never changed or discarded a thing. So it's a wonderful gas-lit Edwardian time-warp, now in the keeping of the National Trust for Scotland.

sights.name: The Museum of Piping
sights.content: The home of the bagpipes is in the former Cowcaddens Free Church. The museum shows 300 years of piping history, mainly showing Scottish bagpipes, but also showing Northumbrian pipes and some from Poland, Hungary, Italy and Spain. The piping

sights.name: Mitchell Library
sights.content: Grand Edwardian Baroque pile endowed by the Mitchell tobacco fortune and opened in 1911. It houses a huge municipal public reference library, with over a million volumes and many more primary source archives for tracing family and civic his

sights.name: Park Circus
sights.content: built around 1860, is the centrepiece of the well-heeled Park District. If they were aiming to recreate Bath, what they got was Edinburgh Scotland Street, with legal brassplates set around a leafy oval - the Montessori School seems inevitab

sights.name: [https://www.glasgow.gov.uk/index.aspx Kelvingrove Park]
sights.content: stretches west, with the River Kelvin running through it. It was laid out in the 1850s when the city's earlier green space, Glasgow Green, became hemmed in by slums. The bandstand was refurbished in 2014, and worthy statues include physicis

sights.name: Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum
sights.content: Magnificent public gallery and museum, opened in 1901 as a legacy of the 1888 International Exhibition. It's in red sandstone, in sort-of Spanish Baroque via St Pancras, and was refurbished in 2006. Extensive collections and displays, well-

sights.name: Kelvin Hall
sights.content: is across the street from Kelvingrove and mirrors its style. This was the city's main event and exhibition venue until SECC opened in 1985, see "Do". It's since been a bit of everything and nowadays is a study and research outpost of the Hu

sights.name: Glasgow University
sights.content: main Gilmorehill campus is a district of half a square mile, bounded to the east by the River Kelvin, to the north by Great Western Road, south by Dumbarton Road, and west by Byres Rd - by Subway use Hillhead. It was founded in 1451, the fo

sights.name: Hunterian Art Gallery
sights.price: Gallery free, Mackintosh House £8 adult, £6 conc, child free
sights.content: It holds a huge collection of work by Whistler, Rennie Mackintosh, the Scottish Colourists and the Glasgow Boys. The Mackintosh House is a reconstruction of the interior of CRM's nearby home, which was lost to university expansion in the 19

sights.name: Hunterian Zoology Museum
sights.content: "Zoology" over the door proclaims the intent, and it's a classical natural history museum where stuffed animals regard you with reproachful glass eyes.

sights.name: Botanic Gardens
sights.hours: Gardens 7AM to dusk, glasshouses noon to 4PM
sights.content: Extensive gardens established in 1842 besides the River Kelvin, with tropical and temperate plants. Its distinctive landmark is the Kibble Palace, a 19th-century wrought-iron temperate glasshouse, rebuilt 2004-06.

sights.name: Fossil Grove
sights.content: The remains of an ancient forest of ''Lepidodendron'', extinct giant quillworts. About 330 million years ago this area flooded with mud, which killed the trees but made casts of their trunks. They were discovered during quarrying in 1887, a

sights.name: St Andrew's Suspension Bridge
sights.content: This elegant footbridge between Hutchisontown on the south river bank and Glasgow Green on the north opened in 1855.

sights.name: Scotland Street School
sights.content: This school, opened in 1906, was Charles Rennie Mackintosh's last major building. It was a wonderful Art Nouveau design (so naturally it was way over budget) and closed in 1979 when the Gorbals slums were demolished and school enrolment fel

sights.name: Riverside Museum
sights.content: Offers an excellent collection of vehicles and models telling the story of transport by land and sea, with a unique Glasgow flavour. Besides the usual rail locomotives, buses, trams, cars and planes, the museum also includes a recreated Sub

sights.name: Govan Stones
sights.content: The present church is from 1888, but there's been a church here since the 6th century, and from about 900 AD it looks to have been the ecclesiastic centre and royal burial ground of the Kingdom of Strathcylde. There's an impressive collecti

sights.name: Fairfield Heritage Centre
sights.content: Govan became the city's main shipbuilding quarter once the Clyde channel was blasted open, and Fairfield was one of its leading companies. Built to impress in 1891, these were the august headquarters of a series of shipbuilders until the la

sights.name: Bellahouston Park
sights.content: The park has a sports centre and an artificial ski slope. The park is often used for open-air concerts and similar events. Its biggest audience to date, of 250,000, was for the visit of Pope John Paul II in 1982. (Benedict XVI drew about a

sights.name: Queen's Cross Church
sights.content: The only church built to a design by Rennie Mackintosh, opened in 1899 for what was then the Free Church. They'd split with the Church of Scotland in 1843 but were reconciled in 1929, so the building continued as C of S until it closed in 1

sights.name: Burrell Collection
sights.content: Sir William Burrell (1861-1958) was a shipping magnate who amassed a huge art collection. He gifted it to the city with the condition that it should be displayed in a nearby yet rural setting, and this was difficult to satisfy until Pollok

sights.name: Titan Crane
sights.content: This stonking great cantilever crane stands 49 m tall. It was built in 1907 to instal massive items such as boilers, engines and gun turrets during ship construction, enabling John Brown & Co to build bigger ships than their competitors. it

foodDrink.name: The Merchant
foodDrink.content: Trad pub serving main dishes.

foodDrink.name: BLOC+
foodDrink.content: Innovative bar with unusual dishes. Separate Vegan/Veggie menu. Live music after 9PM.

foodDrink.name: Panda House
foodDrink.content: Good south-side choice for Cantonese.

foodDrink.name: Lucky Cottage
foodDrink.content: Good reviews for this Chinese takeaway, they also do home deliveries.

foodDrink.name: Eusebi Deli
foodDrink.content: Italian deli and restaurant. Deli has prepared panini, salads, patisserie. Convenient for picnics in the park on a sunny day.

foodDrink.name: Il Pavone
foodDrink.hours: Mon-Wed noon-9PM, Thu-Sat noon-10PM, Sun noon-7:30PM
foodDrink.content: Reliable long-established central Italian.

foodDrink.name: Little Italy
foodDrink.content: Charming relaxing café with vegan options.

foodDrink.name: Paesano Pizza
foodDrink.content: This serves Neapolitan wood-fired pizzas in a cavernous industrial chic restaurant. Their other outlets are at 471 Great Western Road G12 8HL and at 1038 Pollokshaws Rd G41 3EB.

foodDrink.name: Mono
foodDrink.content: Vegan café and bar with live music.

foodDrink.name: Sylvan
foodDrink.content: Excellent range of vegetarian and vegan food.

foodDrink.name: Stereo
foodDrink.content: Vegan pub and live music venue.

foodDrink.name: Hendersons
foodDrink.content: This veggie restaurant, long-established in Edinburgh, now has a Glasgow branch.

foodDrink.name: Shish Mahal
foodDrink.hours: Mon-Thu noon-2PM, 5-10PM, Fri Sat noon-11PM, Sun 3-9PM
foodDrink.content: The Shish has been a steady choice here for over 50 years. With halal options.

foodDrink.name: The Dhabba
foodDrink.content: Authentic North Indian cuisine, great flavour and service.

foodDrink.name: Chillies West End
foodDrink.content: Slick Indian serving in tapas / thali / short-eats style.

foodDrink.name: Angeethi
foodDrink.content: Not just great reviews, but a Michelin star for this excellent restaurant.

foodDrink.name: Ottoman Coffee House
foodDrink.content: Looks nothing from the outside, but within is rich decor and fine food.

foodDrink.name: Opium
foodDrink.content: Slick central restaurant with a variety of Chinese cuisines.

foodDrink.name: Turkiye Efes
foodDrink.content: Good selection of authentic Turkish dishes.

foodDrink.name: Damasqino
foodDrink.content: Relaxed place serving Middle East specialties.

foodDrink.name: Stravaigin
foodDrink.content: Great scores all round for this lively creative gastro-pub.

foodDrink.name: Partick Duck Club
foodDrink.content: Excellent bistro, the duck gets rave reviews. You need to book if you hope for a table inside, walk-ups and dogs welcome outside.

foodDrink.name: Sloans
foodDrink.content: Grand old pub and venue with indoor and outdoor seating. Bistro-type menu.

foodDrink.name: Gamba
foodDrink.content: This award-winning seafood restaurant consistently delights.

foodDrink.name: Thai Siam
foodDrink.content: Good Thai fare, but budget it's not.

foodDrink.name: Mother India
foodDrink.content: This is the original of the chain, established in 1990. It's pricier than most but top-class for quality of food.

foodDrink.name: Killermont Polo Club
foodDrink.content: Smart Indian restaurant in the northwestern suburbs, excellent dining.

foodDrink.name: The Clarence
foodDrink.content: Exceptional quality and a well-earned Michelin award.

foodDrink.name: Ubiquitous Chip
foodDrink.content: Renowned brasserie, great food and setting, booking essential.

foodDrink.name: Red Onion
foodDrink.content: Classy place getting great reviews for modern Scottish cuisine by John Quigley.

foodDrink.name: Chardon d'Or
foodDrink.content: Fancy place headed by Brian Maule, the food lives up to the publicity and price bracket.

foodDrink.name: Cafe Gandolfi
foodDrink.content: A real Glasgow institution, this bistro serves fine food in a relaxed atmosphere. Great food and service.

foodDrink.name: Five March
foodDrink.content: Eclectic fare earning great reviews.

foodDrink.name: Rufus T. Firefly
foodDrink.content: Rock and metal music venue, with good affordable pub food.

foodDrink.name: Horseshoe Bar
foodDrink.content: Good trad pub with food. Its horseshoe-shaped bar is one of the longest continuous bars in Europe. Rock band Travis used to rehearse upstairs before hitting the big time, and one of their Brit Awards is displayed behind the bar.

foodDrink.name: Bier Halle
foodDrink.content: Basement beer hall, pricey, but good beer and pizza.

foodDrink.name: The Flying Duck
foodDrink.content: Bar with vegan menu and live events.

foodDrink.name: Bunker Bar
foodDrink.content: Late spot with food and live music.

foodDrink.name: The State
foodDrink.content: A good ale venue and a cosy proper trad pub.

foodDrink.name: The Hall
foodDrink.content: Lively sports bar, popular with the Glasgow School of Art crowd, with student discounts.

foodDrink.name: Babbity Bowster
foodDrink.content: Slick inn in Merchant City with upstairs dining area and six hotel rooms.

foodDrink.name: The Ben Nevis
foodDrink.content: Snug friendly place with huge selection of whisky and other spirits.

foodDrink.name: Bon Accord
foodDrink.content: Has over 500 whiskies and a huge selection of real ales.

foodDrink.name: Three Judges
foodDrink.content: Great West End pub, good food and selection of Real Ale.

foodDrink.name: Saracen's Head
foodDrink.content: Nicknamed the “Sarry Heid” by locals, this old school pub (founded 1755, although in a different building) lies at the gateway to the Barrowlands area and the East End. Like many pubs in the area it becomes an exclusive haunt of Celtic fans

foodDrink.name: Clockwork Bar
foodDrink.hours: Mon-Wed noon-10PM, Thu, Sun noon-11PM, Fri Sat noon-midnight
foodDrink.content: Spacious modern pub serving from its own microbrewery.

foodDrink.name: West Brewery
foodDrink.content: A restaurant and micro brewery serving German trad food (daily to 9PM) and lager and hefeweizen beers. The tour takes 45 min.

foodDrink.name: Wellpark Brewery
foodDrink.content: Part of Tennent's - that family have been brewing hereabouts since 1556. This is the largest brewery in Scotland and produces Tennent's Lager, their best-seller. They offer a range of tours.

foodDrink.name: Glasgow Distillery Co
foodDrink.content: They make whisky and other spirits - best known is Makar's Cherry Brandy.

foodDrink.name: Clockwork Beer
foodDrink.hours: Mon-Wed noon-10PM, Thu Sun noon-11PM, Fri Sat noon-midnight
foodDrink.content: Pub bistro serving its own craft beers. No tours.

foodDrink.name: Clydeside Distillery
foodDrink.content: This is in the former dock pumphouse; it's owned by Morrison Glasgow Distillers and produces a lowland-style malt. Production began in 2017 so their first whisky came on sale in 2021.

foodDrink.name: Auchentoshan Distillery
foodDrink.content: This is one of a handful of distilleries producing lowland single malt whisky. Auchentoshan is triple distilled and very smooth, unpeaty and somewhat sweet, so it's a good "novice" whisky to try. (Scoffers might say "breakfast whisky".) Cap

sights.name: Myreton Motor Museum
sights.content: Small but fascinating collection of vintage vehicles and motor memorabilia.

sights.name: National Museum of Flight
sights.content: Shows the history of 20th-century flight, with an aircraft collection in four hangars including British Airways Concorde G-BOAA, De-Havilland Comet 4C, Vulcan bomber and Boeing 707.

sights.name: Dirleton Castle
sights.content: Impressive castle dating from about 1240, smashed by Cromwell in 1650. It's set in well-kept gardens.

cityEats.name: Sir Walter Scott's Traditional Tea Room

guideSights.name: Edinburgh Castle
guideSights.note: Iconic fortress perched magnificently on a volcanic rock above the city. The castle has been continuously used for 1100 years and is kept in excellent condition; it's still the ceremonial headquarters of the army in Scotland. Highlights inc

guideSights.name: Camera Obscura
guideSights.note: Over 150 years old, the Camera Obscura projects light from the top of the tower onto a large dish in a dark room below, displaying a panorama of the city. The effect still works on overcast days or at night but is best in sunlight, when you

guideSights.name: Gladstone's Land
guideSights.note: Thomas Gladstone was a wealthy merchant, and in 1617 he had this house refashioned to accommodate his family and to partly rent out. A "Land" means a tall narrow townhouse from the period when Old Town was cramped and the only space for dev

guideSights.name: St Giles
guideSights.note: It's often called a Cathedral, but the Church of Scotland brooks no such episcopal entity, and Charles I dubbing it "cathedral" in 1633 was one reason his head was chopped off. Safer to call it "High Kirk", though they're nowadays lenient w

guideSights.name: Mary King's Close
guideSights.note: Mary King (1590-1644) was a clothes merchant and city burgess. She died the year before plague struck and carried off the rest of her family. In 1753 Royal Exchange, now City Chambers, was built over several closes by demolishing their uppe

guideSights.name: The Peoples' Story Museum
guideSights.note: This is housed in Canongate Tolbooth, the medieval centre for governance and justice (preferably gruesome) as Canongate was a separate jurisdiction until 1856. The museum covers the story of working class life, and of organised labour, from

guideSights.name: Canongate Kirk
guideSights.note: In 1687 James VII (II of England) chucked the Protestants out of Holyrood to convert it to a royal Roman Catholic chapel, the sort of behaviour that got him ousted from the monarchy the following year. The congregation moved to Infirmary St

guideSights.name: Museum of Edinburgh
guideSights.note: Museum of city history in a mustard-hued mansion built in 1570.

guideSights.name: Dunbar's Close Garden
guideSights.note: This close was re-modelled in the 1970s to recreate a 17th-century physic and knot garden, a hidden quiet place in the busy city.

guideSights.name: Scottish Parliament
guideSights.note: A unique building, designed by Spanish Catalan architect Enric Miralles, completed in 2004. It's either a daring showpiece of postmodern architecture or a national embarrassment or a bit of both, time will tell. Parliament meets Tu-Th and y

guideSights.name: Dynamic Earth
guideSights.note: Interactive natural history museum exhibiting the forces and features of our planet: volcanoes, polar ice, rainforests and so on. Opened in 1999, it's a tent-like structure on the former site of a gasworks and brewery.

guideSights.name: Holyrood Palace
guideSights.note: The Palace is a royal residence, closed when the king is here for a week in July and for similar state occasions. It's been repeatedly smashed up and rebuilt, and the present building is mostly from the 1670s. Highlights are the grand stair

guideSights.name: National Library of Scotland
guideSights.note: A venerable reference library, which you need membership to access, but it has public exhibitions about literature. "Treasures" is its permanent exhibition. But don't stumble in here mistaking it for Central Library across the street.

guideSights.name: Central Library
guideSights.note: See Edinburgh#Connect for how to access. The internet stations are in the Learning Centre, and the building houses Central Lending Library, Central Reference Library, Central Children's Library, Edinburgh and Scottish Collections, Art & Des

guideSights.name: National Museum of Scotland
guideSights.note: Superb museum of Scotland's heritage. You enter into the lofty Victorian Grand Gallery, where the millennium clock chimes on the hour. Exhibition halls cover Scottish and world history and culture, science, technology, art and design, and n

guideSights.name: Anatomical Museum
guideSights.note: Large collection of anatomical specimens and life and death masks. Best known is the skeleton of William Burke, hanged in 1829 after he and William Hare killed at least 16 people to sell the bodies for dissection. Limited opening as the are

guideSights.name: St Cecilia's Hall
guideSights.note: Scotland's oldest purpose-built concert hall, opened in 1763 and still in regular use. It hosts the University of Edinburgh collection of historic musical instruments, crafted 16th to 20th century, many of which (such as the Trompette Demil

guideSights.name: Talbot Rice Gallery
guideSights.note: David Talbot Rice (1903-72) was in the louche crowd at Oxford that inspired ''Brideshead Revisited'' and became a distinguished scholar of East Mediterranean and Russian art, with extensive contacts in those parts - how come this fellow was

guideSights.name: Dovecot Studios
guideSights.note: Tapestry studio and gallery housed in the former public baths. There is a cafe, shop, and viewing gallery where you can look down on weavers at work.

guideSights.name: Surgeons' Hall Museums
guideSights.note: The permanent exhibitions are the Pathology Museum, the History of Surgery and the Dental Museum. Not suitable for children under 10 as the exhibits include human remains.

guideSights.name: Edinburgh Central Mosque
guideSights.note: Stately mosque and minaret completed in 1998 in a modern variant of Turkish style. You can generally look in between prayer times.

guideSights.name: City Art Centre
guideSights.note: Four-floor gallery run by the city council. They rotate artwork from their extensive Scottish collection and have changing exhibitions.

guideSights.name: Fruitmarket
guideSights.note: Gallery of contemporary art, refurbished in 2018. From 1936 to the 1970s this was where soft fruit and veg were traded, handy for the trains and delivery vans.

guideSights.name: Stills
guideSights.note: Photography gallery with three exhibitions a year. They also support photographers through courses and hire of equipment, darkroom and digital lab.

guideSights.name: Museum on the Mound
guideSights.note: Museum about money and coins, in the basement of the Palladian pile of the former Bank of Scotland headquarters. Scotland developed a banking sector in the 18th century to support long-distance trade, and still prints its own banknotes.

guideSights.name: Old Calton Cemetery
guideSights.note: Atmospheric Georgian graves, memorials, and funerary ornaments. Memorials include those to the philosopher David Hume (1711-1776), to the Scots who died in the American Civil War, and to the Martyrs of Reform imprisoned or transported for s

guideSights.name: Scott Monument
guideSights.note: Sir Walter Scott (1771-1832) re-invented Scotland. In the late Georgian era, he popularised tales of its medieval and Jacobean tumults, and created the clan tartans you buy on Princes St. This grand Gothic memorial, part cathedral part moon

guideSights.name: National Galleries of Scotland: National
guideSights.note: This holds much of Scotland's fine artwork from Renaissance to 20th century, with changing exhibitions. These rotate seasonally, so an exhibition put on for the Festival typically stays to the end of the year, allowing quieter times to view

guideSights.name: National Galleries of Scotland: Portrait
guideSights.note: Completed in 1890, this is a striking red sandstone neo-Gothic building. It holds portraits of Scots from down the ages, with new faces being added all the time: Billy Connolly and Tilda Swinton mingle with Mary Queen of Scots. The entrance

guideSights.name: Palestine Museum
guideSights.note: A branch of their main museum in Woodbridge Connecticut, this is mostly artwork with exhibitions on the ''Nakhba'' and other events.

guideSights.name: Princes Street Gardens
guideSights.note: The west portion fills the valley beyond the Mound, spanning the railway tracks to the foot of castle crag. The east portion is the terrace around the Scott Monument. They were laid out in the 1820s as private gardens for residents of the s

guideSights.name: The Georgian House
guideSights.note: This townhouse was designed by Robert Adam, completed in 1796 and has been furnished in the style of its first owner John Lamont. Its last private owner the Marquess of Bute also acquired adjacent townhouses and along with the other owners

guideSights.name: Gilbert the Phone Box
guideSights.note: An old red phone box has been kitted out with Edwardian memorabilia, and nicknamed for Sir Giles Gilbert Scott (1880-1960) designer of the box. You can look in the windows anytime, or collect the key for £3 (for Save the Children) from Stew

guideSights.name: James Clerk Maxwell's Birthplace
guideSights.note: Isaac Newton realised that what caused the apple to fall was the very same force moving the moon, planets and stars. James Clerk Maxwell (1831-1879) was born in this house, before the family moved to Kirkcudbright. He was intensely curious

guideSights.name: Dean Bridge
guideSights.note: is best seen from below in Dean Village as you follow the walkway along the stream - from the top it's just a busy thoroughfare. Crossing in four arches 107 ft / 32 m above the stream, it was Telford's last major project. As well as improvi

guideSights.name: National Galleries of Scotland: Modern One
guideSights.note: The original modern art gallery, established in 1960, was in the Botanic Gardens. In 1895 it moved into this neoclassical building, originally a refuge for fatherless children, and in 1999 it expanded across the road into the neoclassical o
guideSights.en: Scottish National Gallery of Modern Art

guideSights.name: Modern Two
guideSights.note: Opposite side of Belford Rd has a slightly smaller collection, but enough to infuriate about one-in-five reviewers, who rage that their kids' drawings stuck on the fridge door are better. A neon sign in the garden reassures all and sundry t

guideSights.name: St Mary's Episcopal Cathedral
guideSights.note: This stonking great neo-Gothic church was completed in 1879, designed by Sir George Gilbert Scott, with the towers added in 1917. It's the senior Episcopal church in Scotland, within the Anglican tradition of bishops (and much else) that th

guideSights.name: St Mary's Metropolitan Cathedral
guideSights.note: The Roman Catholic Cathedral was established as a chapel in 1814 and became a cathedral in 1886 for the archdiocese of Edinburgh and St Andrews. It was designed by James Gillespie Graham in neo-perpendicular style and has undergone several

guideSights.name: Sherlock Holmes
guideSights.note: His creator Sir Arthur Conan Doyle (1859-1930) was born nearby at 11 Picardy Place, to a genteel but impoverished Irish Catholic family. His first Sherlock story was published in 1886. The statue was in storage while the plaza was remodelle

guideSights.name: Royal Botanic Garden
guideSights.note: Impressive gardens with a large collection. Great place to wander around on a sunny day, or to sit and have a picnic. Highlights include the Rock Garden; the 165-m-long herbaceous border, backed by a huge, century-old beech hedge, and the P

guideSights.name: Patriothall Gallery
guideSights.note: Small art gallery and artists studios in the former co-op bakery. The gallery has regular exhibitions of modern art. The studios are open.on one weekend in mid-August and another in late November.

guideSights.name: Fettes College
guideSights.note: Boarding school in an impressive building in the style of a French Château by David Bryce built between 1863 and 1869. It can be seen from far away. Not open for tourists - the best view is looking through the fence from Carrington Road.

guideSights.name: Museum of Scottish Fire Heritage
guideSights.note: Volunteer-run museum within McDonald Road fire station. History of Scottish firefighting from the era of rival commercial fire companies, through early wooden fire engines to more recent appliances.

guideSights.name: Royal Yacht Britannia
guideSights.note: This ship was commissioned in 1954 and was the royal transport and residence on overseas tours until 1997. She has a length of 412 ft / 126 m and oil-fired twin turbines; she was also designed to act as a hospital ship in wartime but was ne

guideSights.name: Trinity House
guideSights.note: Stately neo-classical building of 1818 which is now a maritime museum, but only open for special events. It's built over its predecessor of 1560, which in turn was built over a medieval monastic site. The organisation dates back to 1380, wh

guideSights.name: Upright Gallery
guideSights.note: Small gallery of local artists' work.

guideSights.name: Royal Observatory
guideSights.note: This opened in 1896 to replace the observatory on Calton Hill in New Town (which remained active to 2009 but is now an art exhibition space). The ROE is owned by the Science and Technology Facilities Council and houses the University of Edi

guideSights.name: Craigmillar Castle
guideSights.note: Extensive ruin of a medieval castle, built from the 14th century and abandoned in the 18th. Here was hatched the plot to murder Lord Darnley, the inconvenient husband of Mary Queen of Scots. He was blown up at Kirk O'Field (now the site of

guideSights.name: Edinburgh Printmakers
guideSights.note: Creative centre for printmaking & visual arts, Two free galleries & shop. Vegan Cafe.

guideSights.name: Edinburgh Zoo
guideSights.note: The pandas have returned to China but there's still plenty here. Penguins include gentoo, rockhopper and king, most famously Major General Sir Nils Olav III, Baron of the Bouvet Islands and mascot of the Norwegian King's Guard. Budongo Trai

guideSights.name: Corstorphine Old Parish Church
guideSights.note: The present building is a collegiate church of 1429, becoming a parish church in 1646, and re-modeled in 1828.

guideSights.name: Lauriston Castle
guideSights.note: This 1590s tower house was extended in the 1820s and housed a series of prosperous families. It passed into council ownership in 1926 and the interior has been preserved in its last occupants' plush Edwardian style. Visit by pre-booked guid

guideSights.name: Edinburgh Castle
guideSights.note: Iconic fortress perched magnificently on a volcanic rock above the city. The castle has been continuously used for 1100 years and is kept in excellent condition; it's still the ceremonial headquarters of the army in Scotland. Highlights inc

guideSights.name: Camera Obscura
guideSights.note: Over 150 years old, the Camera Obscura projects light from the top of the tower onto a large dish in a dark room below, displaying a panorama of the city. The effect still works on overcast days or at night but is best in sunlight, when you

guideSights.name: Gladstone's Land
guideSights.note: Thomas Gladstone was a wealthy merchant, and in 1617 he had this house refashioned to accommodate his family and to partly rent out. A "Land" means a tall narrow townhouse from the period when Old Town was cramped and the only space for dev

guideSights.name: St Giles
guideSights.note: It's often called a Cathedral, but the Church of Scotland brooks no such episcopal entity, and Charles I dubbing it "cathedral" in 1633 was one reason his head was chopped off. Safer to call it "High Kirk", though they're nowadays lenient w

guideSights.name: Mary King's Close
guideSights.note: Mary King (1590-1644) was a clothes merchant and city burgess. She died the year before plague struck and carried off the rest of her family. In 1753 Royal Exchange, now City Chambers, was built over several closes by demolishing their uppe

guideSights.name: The Peoples' Story Museum
guideSights.note: This is housed in Canongate Tolbooth, the medieval centre for governance and justice (preferably gruesome) as Canongate was a separate jurisdiction until 1856. The museum covers the story of working class life, and of organised labour, from

guideSights.name: Canongate Kirk
guideSights.note: In 1687 James VII (II of England) chucked the Protestants out of Holyrood to convert it to a royal Roman Catholic chapel, the sort of behaviour that got him ousted from the monarchy the following year. The congregation moved to Infirmary St

guideSights.name: Museum of Edinburgh
guideSights.note: Museum of city history in a mustard-hued mansion built in 1570.

guideSights.name: Dunbar's Close Garden
guideSights.note: This close was re-modelled in the 1970s to recreate a 17th-century physic and knot garden, a hidden quiet place in the busy city.

guideSights.name: Scottish Parliament
guideSights.note: A unique building, designed by Spanish Catalan architect Enric Miralles, completed in 2004. It's either a daring showpiece of postmodern architecture or a national embarrassment or a bit of both, time will tell. Parliament meets Tu-Th and y

guideSights.name: Dynamic Earth
guideSights.note: Interactive natural history museum exhibiting the forces and features of our planet: volcanoes, polar ice, rainforests and so on. Opened in 1999, it's a tent-like structure on the former site of a gasworks and brewery.

guideSights.name: Holyrood Palace
guideSights.note: The Palace is a royal residence, closed when the king is here for a week in July and for similar state occasions. It's been repeatedly smashed up and rebuilt, and the present building is mostly from the 1670s. Highlights are the grand stair

guideSights.name: National Library of Scotland
guideSights.note: A venerable reference library, which you need membership to access, but it has public exhibitions about literature. "Treasures" is its permanent exhibition. But don't stumble in here mistaking it for Central Library across the street.

guideSights.name: Central Library
guideSights.note: See Edinburgh#Connect for how to access. The internet stations are in the Learning Centre, and the building houses Central Lending Library, Central Reference Library, Central Children's Library, Edinburgh and Scottish Collections, Art & Des

guideSights.name: National Museum of Scotland
guideSights.note: Superb museum of Scotland's heritage. You enter into the lofty Victorian Grand Gallery, where the millennium clock chimes on the hour. Exhibition halls cover Scottish and world history and culture, science, technology, art and design, and n

guideSights.name: Anatomical Museum
guideSights.note: Large collection of anatomical specimens and life and death masks. Best known is the skeleton of William Burke, hanged in 1829 after he and William Hare killed at least 16 people to sell the bodies for dissection. Limited opening as the are

guideSights.name: St Cecilia's Hall
guideSights.note: Scotland's oldest purpose-built concert hall, opened in 1763 and still in regular use. It hosts the University of Edinburgh collection of historic musical instruments, crafted 16th to 20th century, many of which (such as the Trompette Demil

guideSights.name: Talbot Rice Gallery
guideSights.note: David Talbot Rice (1903-72) was in the louche crowd at Oxford that inspired ''Brideshead Revisited'' and became a distinguished scholar of East Mediterranean and Russian art, with extensive contacts in those parts - how come this fellow was

guideSights.name: Dovecot Studios
guideSights.note: Tapestry studio and gallery housed in the former public baths. There is a cafe, shop, and viewing gallery where you can look down on weavers at work.

guideSights.name: Surgeons' Hall Museums
guideSights.note: The permanent exhibitions are the Pathology Museum, the History of Surgery and the Dental Museum. Not suitable for children under 10 as the exhibits include human remains.

guideSights.name: Edinburgh Central Mosque
guideSights.note: Stately mosque and minaret completed in 1998 in a modern variant of Turkish style. You can generally look in between prayer times.

guideSights.name: City Art Centre
guideSights.note: Four-floor gallery run by the city council. They rotate artwork from their extensive Scottish collection and have changing exhibitions.

guideSights.name: Fruitmarket
guideSights.note: Gallery of contemporary art, refurbished in 2018. From 1936 to the 1970s this was where soft fruit and veg were traded, handy for the trains and delivery vans.

guideSights.name: Stills
guideSights.note: Photography gallery with three exhibitions a year. They also support photographers through courses and hire of equipment, darkroom and digital lab.

guideSights.name: Museum on the Mound
guideSights.note: Museum about money and coins, in the basement of the Palladian pile of the former Bank of Scotland headquarters. Scotland developed a banking sector in the 18th century to support long-distance trade, and still prints its own banknotes.
